plain_claim: A program (finitely many functions, finitely many parameter slots) satisfies the closure criterion (every idempotent loop graph G = G ; G in the composition closure of its call-site graphs has a strict self-arc) if and only if it is size-change terminating (every infinite path through its call sites, from any function, has an infinitely descending thread).

hypotheses.purpose: A loop that alternates two calls is only visible in a composite graph.

hypotheses.name: h : ClosureCriterion P - component: the self-arc must be strict (forward direction)

hypotheses.name: h : ClosureCriterion P - component: composition does not over-claim strictness, <= ; <= = <= (forward direction)
hypotheses.purpose: Over-claiming strictness manufactures a strict self-arc that no thread justifies.

hypotheses.name: ClosureCriterion P - component: only idempotent loop graphs are tested (converse direction)
hypotheses.purpose: A size-change-terminating program can have non-idempotent loop graphs without self-arcs.

depth_justification: Forward direction (Toy/SCT/Soundness.lean): colour each pair of positions of an infinite call path by the composite of the graphs between them (colours range over the finite list of all graphs, Toy/SCT/Enum.lean), apply Ramsey's theorem for pairs (card ramsey) to get an idempotent loop graph of the closure, and glue the threads given by its strict self-arc into an infinitely descending thread. Converse: via closure-criterion-exact and sct-sound-nat. Both directions rest on the thread semantics of composition (Toy/SCT/Threads.lean).
nonvacuity_witness: The permuting call f(x, y) = f(y, x - 1) (for x > 0) satisfies the criterion and is size-change terminating (its path gSwap, gSwap, ... has the thread x, y, x, y, ...); so does f(x) = f(x - 1).
non_claims: Both sides are properties of the size-change graphs only. Neither says anything about a real program unless its calls respect the graphs (card graphs-must-be-sound).
Size-change termination here quantifies over all infinite paths through the call sites, regardless of guards or reachability; it is not a statement about the paths a real program can actually take.
No complexity or efficiency claim: the closure can be exponentially large, and the problem is PSPACE-hard (Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram, Theorem 5; not formalized here).

Only idempotent loop graphs (G.src = G.dst and G ; G = G) must have a strict self-arc; non-idempotent loop graphs in the closure of a size-change-terminating program may have no self-arc at all (for swapDec: its only call-site graph gSwap = arcsG f0 f0 [(1, 0, .nonstrict), (0, 1, .strict)], that is x' <= y and y' < x, and gSwap3 = gSwap ; gSwap ; gSwap = arcsG f0 f0 [(0, 1, .strict), (1, 0, .strict)], with strict cross-arcs x -> y' and y -> x' and no self-arc, which lies in the closure by comp_pos and inClosure_pos; idempotence_needed_for_converse).

Unrooted model: every function is a possible entry point (as in Ben-Amram, LMCS 2010). Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram (POPL 2001, Definitions 10 and 16) restrict call sequences and the closure to calls reachable from a designated initial function, so a recursive function unreachable from it is ignored there but tested (and possibly rejected) here.

Every function has the same number k of parameter slots; functions with fewer parameters are modelled by slots without arcs. Such slots do not affect the closure, the criterion, size-change termination, consistent runs or checkSCT, but they do affect lexicographic projection measures (card lex-implies-closure-criterion).

Finiteness is essential and is not a removable side condition: finitely many functions are needed for the forward direction, finitely many parameter slots for both directions (counterexamples in the generalized model SCGInf, listed in the hypothesis ledger). Nothing is claimed for systems with infinitely many functions or parameters.

depth_justification: An infinite step sequence yields an infinite consistent run (choose a justifying graph per step); then apply closure-criterion-sound. (Depth labels in this package are marginal: they measure the argument needed given the earlier results of the package.)
nonvacuity_witness: The model of f(x, y) = if x = 0 then 0 else f(y, x - 1) respects the graph x' <= y, y' < x, which satisfies the criterion.
non_claims: StepRespects is an obligation about the real program that this theorem assumes and does not check; a checker that accepts unsound graphs proves nothing (card graphs-must-be-sound).

Termination here means no infinite call sequence of the given relation; it says nothing about non-call sources of divergence (loops inside a function body, partial primitives) unless they are modelled as calls.

Values are natural numbers, and there are finitely many functions and finitely many parameter slots (all three are built into State nf k and each is tight). A real size measure must map into Nat (another well-founded order is not covered here), and nothing is claimed for systems with infinitely many functions or parameters.
No complexity bound (card no-run-length-bound).

Totalized operations need their guards: over Nat, truncated subtraction gives 0 - 1 = 0, so an unguarded call f(x - 1) does not respect x' < x at x = 0 and StepRespects fails (misfit_graphs_counterexample); the same holds for total list operations such as tail [] = [].

Connecting a functional program with nested calls (such as A(m - 1, A(m, n - 1))) to a call relation on evaluated argument states needs a separate call-by-value adequacy argument (Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram, Lemmas 2 and 3); under lazy or non-strict evaluation an infinite call chain need not mean divergence. Neither is modelled.

tier_justification: The graph-based algorithm of Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram (Section 3.2) made precise as a fuel-bounded fixpoint iteration.

depth_justification: Soundness is shallow (a fixpoint list containing the generators and closed under composition contains the closure). nonvacuity_witness: checkSCT accepts the permuting call, which satisfies the criterion.
non_claims: Not an efficient algorithm: the closure may have exponentially many graphs; the decision problem is PSPACE-hard (Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram, Theorem 5), which is not formalized here.

Specification-level cost: the fuel nf * nf * 3^(k*k) + 1 already exceeds 4 * 10^7 for one function with k = 4, and each iteration step scans all pairs of the current list with list-membership tests (cubic in the list length); direct execution or kernel evaluation is impractical except for tiny closures.
The checker computes the full closure. Optimizations such as subsumption change what must be tested (Ben-Amram, LMCS 2010, Section 4.3) and are not covered.
Correctness is relative to the closure criterion, a property of the graphs; it carries no information about whether the graphs are sound for a real program.
The fuel is fixed by the definition; with too little fuel the iteration gives up and the checker rejects (closureIter_neg).
Unrooted: the closure contains the composites of all call paths, from every function (card closure-iff-sct).

hypotheses.purpose: The measure must decrease on every call, justified by the graph alone.

depth_justification: Via closure-criterion-exact: a failing criterion yields an infinite consistent Nat run, along which the measure would decrease lexicographically forever, contradicting well-foundedness of the lexicographic order on Nat^L (lexLt_no_infinite_descent). Single-graph limit: a call site is described by one conjunctive graph. For f(x, y) = f(if y = 0 then x - 1 else x, if y = 0 then 5 else y - 1) every real call decreases (x, y) lexicographically, but the only sound single graph is x' <= x, which fails the criterion unless the call site is split into its two branches (as in ackProg).

plain_claim: In the abstraction, the Ackermann call structure (calls f(x - 1, ?) and f(x, y - 1)) satisfies the closure criterion and has the decreasing lexicographic measure (x, y), yet from the single start state f(1, 0) there are consistent finite runs of every length N, because the call f(x - 1, ?) leaves the second argument unconstrained.
depth_justification: For N >= 1: first the call f(0, N - 1) (allowed because gX leaves y unconstrained), then N - 1 calls decreasing y to 0; for N = 0 the empty run.
positive_control: For f(x) = f(x - 1) (program decLoop, single graph x' < x, which leaves no callee argument unconstrained), every consistent finite run from argument u 0 has at most u 0 steps (FiniteRunFrom decLoop f0 u N -> N <= u 0), so the run-length bound that fails for ackProg holds for this program.
non_claims: The unboundedness comes from one state having infinitely many possible successors in the abstraction (an unconstrained callee argument). A deterministic or finitely branching call relation that terminates has a finite maximum run length from each start state (a classical consequence of Konig's lemma, not formalized here).

The same graphs ackProg also describe the deterministic, linear-time program f(x, y) = if x > 0 then f(x - 1, y + 1) else if y > 0 then f(x, y - 1) else 0 (stepRespects_ackLinStep); the non-primitive-recursive growth of the real Ackermann function comes from its nested call A(m - 1, A(m, n - 1)) supplying the second argument, which this abstraction does not see. No growth rate of any real program is claimed.
A lexicographic measure does not bound run length either; the issue is not specific to size-change termination.
prior_art: A. M. Ben-Amram, "General size-change termination and lexicographic descent", in The Essence of Computation, LNCS 2566, pp. 3-17, 2002, doi:10.1007/3-540-36377-7_1 (verified via Crossref and the publisher's abstract): size-change termination extends and subsumes lexicographic descent; the functions computable by size-change-terminating programs are exactly the multiply-recursive functions.

C. S. Lee, N. D. Jones, A. M. Ben-Amram, "The size-change principle for program termination", POPL 2001, pp. 81-92, doi:10.1145/360204.360210 (bibliographic data verified via Crossref; statements checked in the full text). Definition 11: a program is size-change terminating if every infinite call sequence following its control flow has an infinitely descending thread. Theorem 1: size-change termination implies termination, for size-change graphs that are safe for the program and well-founded data. Theorem 4: the program is not size-change terminating iff the composition closure contains an idempotent G : f -> f with no strict arc x -> x; the forward direction is proved with Ramsey's theorem. Theorems 3 and 5: decidable in polynomial space; PSPACE-hard.
design_question: What exactly does a passed size-change (closure-criterion) check license about a recursive definition, and what does it not license?

tier_justification: Known: Steila (TYPES 2014, Example 37) gives the counting-up program f(x, y) := if x > y then x else f(x + 1, y), which terminates but is not size-change terminating; Heizmann, Jones and Podelski (SAS 2010) show size-change termination is strictly stronger than termination. Restated here for a one-parameter counting-up loop, over all graph sets that describe its calls.
plain_claim: f(x) = if x < 100 then f(x + 1) else 0 terminates, yet every abstraction of it with one function and one parameter slot holding the raw argument x - every P : Prog 1 1 whose graphs describe all of its calls - fails the closure criterion.
depth_justification: The call 0 -> 1 rules out both labels on the only arc of the graph that justifies it, so P contains the empty graph, which is idempotent without a self-arc.
positive_control: Two nearby settings in which the closure criterion does certify termination. (1) On the raw argument, the counting-down loop f(x) = if x = 0 then 0 else f(x - 1) (model decStep s t = (t.1 = s.1 ∧ 0 < s.2 0 ∧ t.2 0 = s.2 0 - 1)) is certified: the one-function, one-slot program decLoop with the single graph x' < x describes all of its calls (StepRespects decLoop decStep), decLoop passes the closure criterion, and decStep terminates. (2) The counting-up loop itself is certified once the slot holds the size norm 100 - x instead of the raw argument x: every call s -> t of countUpStep respects the graph x' < x of decLoop on the values 100 - x (that is, 100 - x' < 100 - x), and decLoop passes the closure criterion.
non_claims: Rejection by the checker is not evidence of divergence.

The impossibility fixes nf = 1, k = 1 and identifies the single slot with the raw argument x. Within plain size-change graphs (no difference constraints) the loop is certified as soon as the abstraction changes: measured by the size norm 100 - x every call respects x' < x (countUp_size_norm_positive_control); a second slot tracking 100 - x, or splitting the 101 values into acyclic control points, also works (not formalized).
Richer abstractions (difference constraints, guards) can also certify this loop, and Lean's own inference accepts it via a measure 100 - x derived from the guard (observation recorded in prior art).
prior_art: S. Steila, "An intuitionistic analysis of size-change termination", TYPES 2014, LIPIcs 39, pp. 288-307, 2015, doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2014.288 (full text consulted). Example 37 (Section 6): f(x, y) := if x > y then x else f(x + 1, y) is not SCT, since its only graph is idempotent with no decreasing edge, yet it terminates. Section 1 attributes to Heizmann, Jones and Podelski ("Size-change termination and transition invariants", SAS 2010, pp. 22-50) the result that size-change termination is strictly stronger than termination.

tier_justification: Ramsey's theorem for pairs (infinite version, finitely many colours) restated over Nat; included as an auxiliary statement because the soundness direction of the closure criterion is classically proved from it.
plain_claim: Auxiliary lemma (not a headline result of this package): For any colouring col of the pairs m < n of natural numbers whose colours all lie in a finite list S, there is a strictly increasing h : Nat -> Nat and a colour a with col (h m) (h n) = a for all m < n.

hypotheses.name: hS : ∀ m n, m < n → col m n ∈ S (finitely many colours)
hypotheses.purpose: With infinitely many colours there need not be any homogeneous infinite set.

depth_justification: Proved by iterated infinite pigeonhole (Toy/SCT/Ramsey.lean): repeatedly pick a candidate position and shrink the infinite candidate set to the positions whose pair with it has one colour, then apply pigeonhole once more to the chosen colours. Needs explicit construction of infinite sequences by choice; no library support.
nonvacuity_witness: The parity colouring (m + n) % 2 takes values in [0, 1]; h n = 2 n is homogeneous of colour 0.
non_claims: Only the infinite version for pairs and finitely many colours; no finite Ramsey numbers, no hypergraph version, no bounds.
The homogeneous colour a is not computed; the statement is purely existential.
It is not claimed that Ramsey's theorem is necessary for size-change soundness; intuitionistic alternatives exist in the literature (Vytiniotis, Coquand and Wahlstedt 2012; Steila 2015).

Proof-theoretic strength is not addressed: the size-change characterization does not need the full strength of Ramsey's theorem for pairs (over RCA_0 the SCT criterion is equivalent to Sigma^0_2 induction and needs only a triangle corollary of Ramsey's theorem; Frittaion, Steila and Yokoyama, TAMC 2017). The package proves the full infinite version for pairs because it is simple to state and to apply.
